comment: A few points. You DO have neighbors, albeit separated by high hedges and trees. Zillow says it was built in 2008, so it probably has some hurricane mitigation.  But you are right on the water and not far above sea level. Taxes are just shy of $800k though anyone looking at this place will not be worried about that. Insuring this place will be challenging, and very expensive (if you can get it). And then there is the routine maintenance and upkeep. Staff (servants), security, grounds keepers, utilities and the routine bills everyone has x 1000. All of which said this is a nice place if you want to live like Florida's Lord of Downton Abbey and have the bank to support that lifestyle. The problem is that not many people with that kind of money live like this anymore. A hundred years ago, if you were wealthy you were expected to flaunt it. With a few exceptions (Donald Trump and various "new money" celebrities), most people who have money prefer to live comfortably while eschewing the conspicuous consumption of the Gilded Age which this place is obviously intended to emulate. William K. Vanderbilt would have been very happy spending a few weeks or months a year here. Not sure how many of his modern day counterparts would.

author: @tobias-hastings
comment:
The majority of spaces in the home feel amazing but there were a few areas that need some adjustments.  All of the corridors feel very small compared to the rooms they are coming from and going to (example: entrance area to the office / great room), which felt claustrophobic, stuffy, and like a poor use of the space; none of them needed all the cupboards and other items that felt forced into them to do something with them.  Similarly, the entrance area and the area at the bottom of the stairs leading into the lower level were a good height but the walls felt way too close.

With those out of the way all of the views from the windows we saw were amazing.  The great room, the courtyard, the kitchen/dining/family room, the backyard and pool, everything about the entertainment floor, most of the guest suites and the primary bedroom and bathroom, felt open and inviting and like there was room to just stand there and breathe, to take it all in.



A lot of the $150m price tag will be because of the location, but anyone buying this property should consider setting some money aside to making renovations so that the few problem areas feel as open as the rest.

author: @CC_Foster
comment: Thought I would share a detail on how the Steel Infrastructure is done if anyone is interested.  We did a big steel project as part of our home.  The steel is all done by a separate steel fabricator of course.  The Architect provides the CAD drawings, those go the the Steel fab.  The Final Steel shows up on site, sort of like an erector set, all the pieces are labeled and they use the drawings to assemble the I-Beams, the Steel connectors, all the way down to the bolts.  The I-Beams look like they are Pre Drilled at the Fab Plant with holes in the Beam "Channel", but they are actually punched.  Ours were 2 holes, top and bottom,  every 12 inches.  This allows our builder to place a large 2x12 inside the I-Beam channel.   Then they drill thru all the holes from the other side of the I-Beam thru the wood.  Then put another 2x12 on the other side of the I-Beam and drill back thru.  Then they Bolt the 2x12 together in the I-Beam channel.  So, they basically make a wood sandwich in the channel of the I-Beam.  That way they can use traditional Joists and Joist hangars for the transition from Steel to Wood.   I had never seen it done before and I am an Engineer so it was pretty awesome to see it.   We needed a 34 foot open span and with the super large accordion doors we went with, the deflection spec was I think 1/8", so it took some serious steel work.

author: @Maneyh
comment:
As far as I'm aware, Turks & Caicos is only one place on earth that beats the Bahamas in terms of taxes levels. In terms of a complete lack of taxes, Turks & Caicos has everything that Bahamas has, but they decided to take property tax out of the equation as well. That is zero taxation in literally every single way for the people who live there! The only tax money that Turks & Caicos makes comes from tourism and other outside sources.

With it's small size, Turks & Caicos basically serves as one large and very wealthy community out in the ocean, with a total of 13 private residences (according to Enes). I still prefer the Bahamas personally due to it's significantly larger size, and thus access to other things in addition to only private residential property, such as larger stores, cars and city life. The extremely low elevation levels across the entire Turks & Caicos island is also concerning due to rising sea levels.

Plus, it's not as if the property tax really matters at all to the wealthy individuals that choose to move to the Bahamas anyways, as it's based purely off of property value and not personal net worth anyways, and is thus gonna come to such a insignificant and unnoticeable amount. For that reason, I deem the Bahamas superior as a place to live due to literally every other factor. Living in Turks & Caicos, you would be quite isolated from the rest of the world after all. But that would just be my personal opinion.

That house is amazing, however that trellis in the entry way is going to end up twisted and warped by the time that wood is "cured" (in anywhere from 2-6 years). I've built so many things with sappy wood like that (from places like Home Depot and Lowes) that started out perfect and ended up curing so crooked, it looked like a blind child with no arms built it. Of course buying kiln-dried wood probably would have cost a bit more, but I think that would have been worth it for the longevity of the wood. Stains and sealants can't penetrate the wood and do their job if the sap is already soaking up the wood and freshly oozing out like that. Just how I would have done it, but otherwise the house looks great so far.

Also, that AC Cobra is beautiful but if I lived there, all the doors and windows would be open all the time and any vehicle parked there would rust to pieces!
